newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan budget gap must be curbed - central bank.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan budget gap must be curbed - central bank.

text.p: Pakistan's central bank warned Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government, in a report to parliament on Wednesday, that its economic reforms could be imperilled unless it can curb the chronic budget deficit.

The State Bank of Pakistan said the government's structural reforms would greatly enhance the economy's efficiency in the medium and long term after what it called a dismal performance in fiscal 1996/97 (July/June).
However, the economy "needs to be handled with care during the transitional period", the report cautioned.
"In particular, continuation of a large budget deficit could endanger the course of economic reforms," it said.
Former prime minister Benazir Bhutto's government vowed to reduce the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996/97 from 6.3 percent the previous year.
The pledge was part of conditions for an International Monetary Fund standby loan, which has since been suspended.
Sharif's government, which took office in February after winning elections, rejected the target as unrealistic and now forecasts this year's budget deficit at 6.1 percent of GDP.
On May 29 its policy-making National Economic Council set a budget deficit target of five percent for 1997/98.
Sharif wants a new medium-term loan from the IMF, which is likely to send a mission to Islamabad in July, assuming end-year targets are met and the budget proves satisfactory.
The 1997/98 budget, due to be unveiled on June 14, "should set the tone in changing the direction of fiscal management in Pakistan", the central bank report said.

"It is obvious that what is needed is a combination of long-term structural reforms and short-term stabilisation measures to help create a basis for the resumption of Pakistan's sustained economic growth within the framework of financial stability and balance of payments viability," it said.
The bank report said a "persisting fiscal imbalance" was at the root of most of Pakistan's macroeconomic problems.

"The country's inability to meet the targets for reducing the budget deficit acts as a major impediment to the achievement of objectives of lowering inflation, promoting savings and investment, ensuring the competitiveness of exports and accelerating long-term growth," it added.
It asked the government to raise its revenues and reduce expenditure to reduce the fiscal deficit.

The bank endorsed a government estimate of 3.1 percent GDP growth this year, against 4.1 percent last year. This would be second lowest growth rate in a decade, after 2.3 percent in 1992/93 when severe river floods caused havoc with crops.

Agriculture is again likely to suffer a sharp slowdown to 0.7 percent growth from 5.3 percent last year, largely owing to a disappointing cotton crop. Manufacturing growth is likely to experience a decline of 1.4 percent, the report said.
